questions.stem: Into what two kinds of structure does Dimensional Data Modelling organise data?
options: Facts (quantitative measures) and dimensions (descriptive attributes)
Hubs and satellites
Anchors and ties
Nodes and edges
Keys and values
questions.explanation: Dimensional modelling structures data into facts, which are quantitative measures, and dimensions, which are descriptive attributes, to support reporting and BI.

questions.stem: What is the primary goal of dimensional modelling?
options: Eliminating redundancy at all costs
Delivering a business-friendly, performance-optimised structure for fast and intuitive access to information
Enforcing referential integrity across the enterprise
Supporting fine-grained operational updates
Capturing every attribute change on its own timeline
questions.explanation: Dimensional modelling focuses on making data easy to query, aggregate and understand rather than on eliminating redundancy.

questions.stem: Which two questions do facts and dimensions answer together?
options: How is the data stored, and who owns it?
When was it recorded, and when was it valid?
What happened, and under what circumstances did it happen?
Which node connects to which, and how many hops?
What is the key, and what is the value?
questions.explanation: Facts answer what happened and dimensions answer under what circumstances it happened.

options: Dimensions are partially normalised into sub-dimensions
Facts are stored as events
Every dimension references a geography table
The fact table connects directly to denormalised dimension tables with minimal joins
Every table is in 6NF
questions.explanation: In a star schema the fact table connects directly to denormalised dimension tables, producing a simple, high-performance structure that is the most common dimensional design.

questions.stem: In a snowflake schema, what might a Customer dimension reference?
options: An event stream
A fact table
A hub table
A JSON document
A separate Geography table
questions.explanation: In a snowflake schema dimensions are partially normalised into sub-dimensions; for example a Customer dimension may reference a separate Geography table.

questions.stem: How does dimensional modelling relate to normalisation?
options: It intentionally denormalises data to optimise usability and query performance
It requires full compliance with 3NF
It targets 6NF for temporal accuracy
It applies DKNF constraints to dimensions
It is identical to Inmon's 3NF approach
questions.explanation: Unlike highly normalised relational models, dimensional models intentionally denormalise; snowflake schemas reintroduce limited normalisation but full compliance is not the objective.

questions.stem: Which measures does the example Fact_LoanApproval table contain?
options: CustomerID, Name and Segment
LoanAmount, InterestRate, ApprovalFlag and ApprovalCount
Day, Month, Quarter and Year
Branch and ExperienceLevel
LoanType and Secured/Unsecured
questions.explanation: The Fact_LoanApproval table contains measures such as LoanAmount, InterestRate, ApprovalFlag and ApprovalCount, surrounded by Customer, Officer, Product and Date dimensions.

questions.stem: Which question is given as an example that business users can easily answer with a dimensional loan model?
options: Which officers are connected to high-risk customers?
What was the interest rate as of 14 January?
Total Approved Loan Amount by Customer Segment and Quarter
Which loan documents embed the same customer?
Which events must be replayed to rebuild the loan?
questions.explanation: Example questions include Total Approved Loan Amount by Customer Segment and Quarter, Approval Rate by Branch and Product Type, and Average Interest Rate by Officer Experience Level.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a strength of dimensional modelling?
options: Intuitive structure
Fast aggregation performance
Strong alignment with reporting needs
Suitability for transaction processing and fine-grained operational updates
Natural scaling by adding new fact tables or dimensions
questions.explanation: Dimensional modelling is less suitable for transaction processing or fine-grained operational updates; its strengths lie in intuitive structure, fast aggregation and reporting alignment.

questions.stem: To which modelling family does dimensional modelling belong?
options: The ensemble family alongside Data Vault and Anchor
The pre-relational family alongside hierarchical and network models
The semantic family alongside ontologies
The NoSQL family alongside document stores
An OLAP-oriented approach rooted in denormalisation, separate from the ensemble family
questions.explanation: Dimensional modelling is not part of the ensemble family (Data Vault, Anchor, Focal Point); it is an OLAP-oriented approach rooted in denormalisation.
